extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, and legal practitioners concerned with copyright and publication law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of legal rules governing copyright in engravings/prints, patterns for linen, sculptures/models, and literary works, including ownership, statutory formalities, remedies, limitations, evidence, and assignment. Aimed at explaining statutory construction and remedies available at law and in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in prints vested in the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: The property in prints is vested in the artist; a person cannot monopolize a print which has been made for him without having assisted in its design or formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person merely procures another to make an engraving from his design he may claim copyright; but if the print was made for him without his assistance in design or formation, he cannot monopolize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written consent requirement for lawful copying of prints
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a print can be copied with impunity, it is necessary to obtain 'the consent of the proprietor thereof in writing, signed by him in the presence of two witnesses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of such written consent makes copying, printing, reprinting, publishing, selling or otherwise disposing of the print actionable under the statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee may maintain action for pirated prints
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignee of a print may maintain an action against any person who has pirated it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language and case law support that rights in prints pass to assignees for enforcement of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of piracy for engravings/prints
rubrics_metrics.description: A piracy is committed if any person 'in any manner copy in the whole or in part by varying, adding to, or diminishing from, the main design' of any print whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A facsimile (exact copy) is gross infringement; but the statute also reaches partial copying effected by variation, addition, or diminution from the main design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury assessment of whether similarity is copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject of an engraving is a general one, the jury must consider whether each work was engraved from the general subject or whether the similitude arises from accident or the nature of the subject, or whether one print is merely a copy of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors: whether designs were sketched from the same text, whether similarity is due to the nature of the subject (e.g., a plant), or whether actual copying occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller/importer liability for selling pirated prints
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one who sells or imports for sale any pirated copies of an engraving is liable to the penalties inflicted by the statutes, even if he did not know they were copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later statutes (e.g. 17 Geo. III. c. 57.) omit the word 'knowing,' indicating a seller can be liable without knowledge. A seller of a copy that comes 'so near the original' is liable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for 'copy' / colourable variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy is that which comes so near to the original as to give to every person seeing it the idea created by the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colourable or trifling variations will not avoid liability if the overall impression conveyed to an ordinary observer is that of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and forfeitures for piracy of prints
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalty includes forfeiture of the plates on which the prints are copied, every sheet on which the engraving has been printed (to be destroyed), and a fine (e.g., five shillings) for every print found in custody; one moiety to the king and the other to the informer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes impose both forfeiture and pecuniary penalties and provide for private informers sharing a portion of the penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special action on the case for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (17 Geo. III. c. 57.) a special action on the case may be brought to recover such damages as a jury may give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a civil remedy in addition to statutory forfeitures and enables recovery of damages assessed by jury or by writ of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limitation periods for piracy actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions for anything done in pursuance of certain prints statutes (e.g., 8 Geo. II. c. 13. and 7 Geo. III. c. 38.) must be brought within six calendar months after the fact committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all later statutes include a limitation; check the specific statute (e.g., 17 Geo. III. c. 57. omits such limitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration drafting for partial copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations should be drawn for copying part as well as for copying the whole since pirated copies often resemble originals in particular parts and differ in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful pleading is required to allege copying of parts as well as entire works to match factual patterns of piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant pleading options in piracy suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant is permitted to plead the general issue and to give any special matter in evidence under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special matter (e.g., license, prior sale, ownership claims) may be introduced under the general issue plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary sufficiency: prints as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to produce the plate itself; one of the prints taken from the original plate is sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evidence rules: a print from the original plate may prove ownership; however, keeping the original proprietor's name on the print is recommended as the best evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferability of retaining first proprietor's name on print
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems the best way to continue the name of the first proprietor on the print; it is doubtful whether a plate with the name of an assignee (though dated correctly) is good evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip to preserve evidence and facilitate proof of title: keep the original proprietor's name on the printed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable relief (injunction) available in piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although equity proceedings are not mentioned in the statutes, the Court of Chancery will in aid of the statutes interpose with an injunction to prevent or stop the injury sustained by the artist from a piracy of his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff may seek injunctive relief in equity in addition to statutory remedies; equity will act to prevent ongoing injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs allocation in piracy and special actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff succeeds in suing for penalties, he is entitled to his full costs; if he succeeds in the special action on the case, he is to have double costs of suits. If plaintiff is nonsuited or discontinues, full costs are allowed to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different procedures yield different cost consequences; successful penalties suits and special actions can lead to full or double costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory monopoly for patterns for linen (novelty and marking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes grant a limited monopoly to the proprietor of any 'new and original pattern for printing linens, cottons, calicos, or muslins,' to commence from the day of first publishing, which 'must be truly printed with the name of the printer or proprietor at each end of every such piece of linen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements for protection: novelty/originality of pattern, correct marking with name (and in some cases date), and compliance with statutory formalities determine entitlement to the limited monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-date and name requirements for patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether it is necessary to comply with the statute as to the date and name in order to support an action: court held that plaintiff must prove the date was on the linen to entitle him to a verdict, and declaration can be aided after verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although pleadings may be aided after verdict, plaintiffs should ensure statutory marking (date/name) is present and proved at trial to establish entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and transfer rules for patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Property in patterns is given to the inventors or proprietors; no mention of assigns is made, but a power to assign may be inferred; purchaser may be exempted from action if legitimately bought; sale of a copied pattern may not be an offence if vendor did not know it was pirated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment formalities and purchaser-protection doctrines differ from prints; seller's knowledge may affect liability differently for patterns vs. engravings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy and procedure for pattern piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedy for infringement of patterns is a special action in the case to recover damages; time limited for bringing actions under these acts is six months; defendant may plead general issue; equity proceedings may aid; costs as in other statutory provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural parallels with other print statutes: civil action for damages, short limitation period, and availability of equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for sculptures, models, copies, and casts
rubrics_metrics.description: Property is vested in the first maker of all original sculptures, models, copies and casts (for specified statutory terms—e.g., 14 years with potential extension for an additional 14 years); proprietor should cause name and date to be put on them before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute enumerates many items and vests exclusive rights for a fixed term; insertion of name/date before publication is a statutory condition for protection by analogy to patterns and prints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser's exemption for legitimate acquisition of a sculpture/model
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchaser of any original sculpture or model shall be exempted from an action for copying, casting, or vending the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bona fide purchaser who acquires legitimately may not be liable; sellers who knowingly deal in pirated items remain subject to the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory action and limitation for sculptures/models piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Enactment against piracy of sculptures/models gives proprietor or his assignee an action on the case for damages (with double costs) to be brought within six months against those who imitate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirements mirror those for other artistic works: short limitation, availability of damages, and doubled costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's absolute property in manuscripts pre-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: An author has an absolute property independent of statute law over his work whilst it continues in manuscript; mere delivery of the manuscript to the printer does not divest the author, since consent to print must be in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors retain control of unpublished manuscripts; written consent required to permit printing—verbal permissions or possession alone do not transfer right to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of copyright and statutory terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory durations have varied: earlier statutes confined copyright to 14 years (with a possible second 14-year term), later statutes provided for 28 years and, for later enactments, extension to the life of the author if he survives the statutory period; transitional rules affect works published before changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the applicable statute by publication date and whether the author survived statutory periods; resulting terms and retrospective effects are governed by statute and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of subject matter (obscenity, libel, blasphemy) on copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: A work is necessarily destroyed as property by its subject being blasphemous, seditious, or libellous, or by its being obscene or immoral; an author may refuse to supply a manuscript if justly apprehensive that its contents will subject him to punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illicit or criminal content may strip a work of copyright protection and justify refusal to publish; courts consider content's legality when assessing entitlement to protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities for assignment to enable enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment of a copyright, and of engravings and models, must be in writing to enable the assignee to protect his interest either at law or in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written assignments provide clear title for litigation and equitable relief; parol assignments are risky though equity may sometimes intervene depending on conduct and evidence (e.g., receipt of purchase money).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignment on resulting term (benefit to assignee)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the general assignment of all his right in a work, the assignee has the benefit of the resulting term for the life of the author when he survives the statutory term (e.g., twenty-eight years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments may carry with them statutory resulting terms; the precise effect depends on statutory language and timing of assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to prove assignment/ownership for relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence such as production of a receipt for the price of the copyright may be insufficient; affidavits must state that the purchase was from the author; but equity has sometimes granted relief on parol assignment where defendants had received purchase money and permitted the plaintiff to print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff should present clear written title or credible evidentiary proof tracing title from the author; defects in proof can lead to nonsuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise and transmissibility of copyright (testamentary and execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is a personal chattel and may be devised; a manuscript will pass to the author's executors; copyright may become vested in personal representatives under some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat copyright as transmissible property for wills and administration, but note limitations (e.g., unpublished manuscript under execution may be contentious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of copyright by authorial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An author may by his conduct abandon his work and give to the public a power to publish his book before the usual time of copyright has transpired, though there is little authority and courts would require proof of such intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment is fact-specific and hard to prove; statements such as 'I will make a present of this work to you to publish' may evidence abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's prerogative and special privileges for certain works
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain works (Acts of Parliament, proclamations, orders of council, liturgies, and the Bible) are said to fall under the King's prerogative, with patents granted historically to printers; the existence and extent of such prerogative have been questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special patents (e.g., King's printer, university privileges) historically affect printing rights for particular classes of works; their validity and scope are subject to legal debate and judicial scrutiny.
